paragraphs: Generating a molecular structure with attractive properties does not establish that chemists can make it. This paper addresses that gap by organizing molecule generation around a proposed chemical process. Instead of proposing only a finished structure, the model selects starting materials and predicts the molecule that their reaction would produce.

The starting materials come from a pool of commercially available molecules. The generative model proposes a collection of these reactants, and a reaction model predicts how they combine. This design introduces information about reactions into the generation process, giving chemists both a proposed product and starting materials whose suitability they can investigate.

The authors show that the approach generates diverse, valid, and unique molecules, attributing these properties to the useful structure imposed by modeling reactions. They also apply it to retrosynthesis: finding reactants predicted to produce a specified target. The contribution is a way to connect molecular proposals with assessable synthesis routes; the abstract does not establish that every predicted reaction succeeds in practice.
neurips-2019-a-model-to-search-for-synth.tldr: A molecule generator selects commercially available reactants and predicts their products, making proposed synthesis routes available for inspection.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a probability distribution on the simplex, the space of nonnegative vectors whose entries sum to one. Such vectors can describe how a total amount is divided among alternatives. The construction combines the Kumaraswamy distribution with an ordered stick-breaking process, which builds a vector by successively allocating portions of a remaining total.

The authors study the distribution's mathematical properties and prove that it is exchangeable under the same conditions as the Dirichlet distribution. Exchangeability means that reordering the components does not change their joint distribution. Like the Dirichlet, the new distribution can represent sparse allocations, where relatively few components receive most of the total.

Its key computational feature is an exact, closed-form reparameterization, which makes it suitable for deep variational Bayesian modeling. The authors demonstrate its usefulness in several semi-supervised auto-encoding tasks. They report competitive performance across those tasks while retaining simple models, explicit probabilistic descriptions, and training without adversarial methods. The stated result is competitiveness, rather than universal superiority over alternative distributions.
neurips-2019-a-new-distribution-on-the-s.tldr: A new simplex distribution combines sparsity and conditional exchangeability with an exact reparameterization for variational auto-encoding.

paragraphs: Training a deep network can produce different parameter settings with similarly low loss. Mode connectivity describes the observation that these solutions, at least those found by gradient-based training, can often be joined by simple paths along which loss barely changes. Sometimes a path needs only two straight segments, despite the complexity of the network.

This paper develops mathematical explanations for that behavior in realistic multilayer networks. The explanation assumes properties of well-trained networks such as dropout stability and noise stability. These properties describe forms of robustness to perturbations and had also been identified in work on why trained networks generalize beyond their training examples.

The resulting account connects the geometry of low-loss solutions with stability properties of the networks themselves. It explains how different successful parameter settings can belong to connected regions without requiring a large increase in loss along the connecting route. Experiments are presented to check the theory. The explanation remains conditional on the stated stability assumptions; it is not a claim that every pair of network optima admits such a path.
neurips-2019-explaining-landscape-connec.tldr: The paper explains low-loss paths between trained multilayer networks under stability assumptions and presents experiments checking the theory.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization where the objective is convex but the allowed solutions form a nonconvex set. Its central example requires the solution to be an output of a neural network. A generator therefore acts as a prior: optimization searches among what the network can produce, rather than over every possible value of the variable.

The authors propose a linearized version of the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, or ADMM, for this setting. Their convergence rates depend on geometric properties of the generator. They also show that feedforward architectures have the required properties under assumptions described as mild, connecting the analysis to a commonly used family of networks.

The approach is motivated by generative-model applications including compressive sensing, denoising, and resistance to adversarial examples. Its practical appeal is that it can efficiently accommodate nonsmooth objectives and exploit efficient procedures for partially minimizing the problem. The authors state that these features make it faster than gradient descent in many practical scenarios. Both the rate guarantees and the speed claim have a specific scope, rather than covering every generator and objective.
neurips-2019-fast-and-provable-admm-for-.tldr: A linearized ADMM method optimizes with neural-generator constraints, with geometry-dependent guarantees and practical advantages for nonsmooth objectives.

paragraphs: Linear regression with a p-norm objective appears in applications including sparse recovery, semi-supervised learning, and signal processing. Generic convex solvers can be slow for these problems. Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares, or IRLS, offers a simple alternative that repeatedly solves weighted least-squares problems, but existing versions often diverge when p exceeds three.

The paper proposes p-IRLS and proves geometric convergence for every finite p of at least two. Geometric convergence means the error decreases at a multiplicative rate as iterations progress. This resolves the convergence question for p greater than three within the proposed algorithm, while retaining the implementation simplicity that makes IRLS attractive.

The authors also guarantee a high-accuracy solution in a sublinear number of iterations. Their experiments perform better than the theoretical bounds suggest and report speeds 10–50 times those of the standard Matlab/CVX implementation used for comparison. They further report the fastest performance among the available implementations in the high-accuracy regime. These findings combine a broad convergence guarantee over the stated p range with empirical evidence about practical solver speed.
neurips-2019-fast-provably-convergent-ir.tldr: p-IRLS provides geometric convergence for p-norm regression with finite p ≥ 2 and strong empirical speed in high-accuracy solving.

paragraphs: Anchor-based object detectors must decide which candidate anchors should be responsible for each labeled object during training. Common assignment rules restrict those matches using geometric overlap between an anchor and the object's box. FreeAnchor replaces this hand-designed assignment with a learned matching approach that permits more flexible object-anchor associations.

The paper formulates detector training as maximum likelihood estimation and designs a likelihood specifically for detection. This objective connects matching with the two tasks a detector must perform: identifying an object's class and locating it accurately. The intended result is to learn features that explain objects well on both dimensions, rather than letting overlap rules alone determine their training assignments.

FreeAnchor can be incorporated into convolutional object detectors as a plug-in training approach. Experiments on MS-COCO report consistent improvements over the compared counterparts, with margins the authors describe as significant. The finding supports learned matching as a useful part of detector training in those experiments. Its contribution concerns how anchors acquire responsibility for objects, alongside the classification and localization behavior that responsibility encourages.
neurips-2019-freeanchor-learning-to-matc.tldr: FreeAnchor learns object-anchor matches through a detection likelihood and consistently improves the compared detectors on MS-COCO.

paragraphs: Equivariant image networks are designed so that transforming an input produces a corresponding transformation in their internal features. This paper provides a general description of convolutions equivariant to the planar Euclidean group E(2) and its subgroups. The setting includes the rotations and reflections that motivate many existing equivariant convolutional architectures.

Within the steerable CNN framework, rules describing how features transform impose constraints on convolution kernels. The authors show that constraints involving arbitrary group representations can be reduced to constraints for irreducible representations, the simpler components from which representations are built. They then give a general solution to the resulting kernel-space constraints.

This mathematical framework supports both previously proposed architectures and new ones, which the authors implement and compare extensively. They also replace ordinary convolutions with E(2)-steerable convolutions and report substantial gains on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and STL-10. The contribution therefore links a unified construction method with empirical evidence that these symmetry-respecting layers can improve image classification in the evaluated settings, while serving as replacements for existing convolution layers.
neurips-2019-general-e-2-equivariant-ste.tldr: A general theory constructs E(2)-equivariant convolutions and supports architectures that improve performance on three image benchmarks.

paragraphs: Incremental aggregated gradient methods are used in network optimization and machine learning. The paper identifies restrictive aspects of their existing theory: convergence results require strong convexity, focus on linear rates, and tie the permitted step size to the strong-convexity constant. When that constant is small, this restriction can force very small updates.

The authors introduce a general proximal incremental aggregated gradient scheme that includes the basic method and several existing algorithms. They use this broader framework to establish additional convergence results, including analysis of nonconvex problems and sublinear convergence rates for objective values. This expands the range of behavior the theory can describe beyond the earlier strongly convex setting.

The analysis also provides convergence guarantees for much larger step sizes and addresses cases with noise. In addition, the paper develops a line-search strategy and proves its convergence. These are distinct extensions within a shared algorithmic framework: broader problem settings, less restrictive update choices, and a justified mechanism for selecting steps. Sublinear rates here extend the available guarantees; they do not imply faster convergence than linear rates.
neurips-2019-general-proximal-incrementa.tldr: A general proximal aggregated-gradient framework extends convergence analysis to nonconvex and noisy settings, larger steps, and line search.

paragraphs: Glyce investigates how the visual forms of Chinese characters can improve language representations. The paper identifies two obstacles: individual glyphs may offer limited pictographic evidence, and standard vision models generalize poorly on character images. Its approach combines richer character imagery with a network and training setup designed for this particular kind of visual information.

First, Glyce incorporates historical scripts, including bronzeware and seal scripts, along with traditional Chinese characters. Second, it introduces tianzege-CNN, a convolutional architecture tailored to character images. Third, it adds image classification as an auxiliary task during multitask learning to improve generalization. Together, these choices make glyph information an explicit component of character representation.

The authors report consistent improvements over word- or character-ID representations across a broad range of Chinese language tasks. Combined with BERT, Glyce achieves new state-of-the-art results on several evaluated tasks, spanning classification, tagging, parsing, and semantic role labeling. Reported examples include an OntoNotes named-entity recognition F1 of 81.6, 1.5 points above BERT, and 99.8% accuracy on Fudan text classification.
neurips-2019-glyce-glyph-vectors-for-chi.tldr: Glyce combines historical character images, specialized convolutions, and auxiliary image classification to improve Chinese language representations.

paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised learning uses relationships among nodes to learn from a mixture of labeled and unlabeled examples. Much of its existing literature assumes that labeled nodes are sampled randomly. This paper examines a more difficult situation: whether a node receives a label depends on the response that is unobserved when the label is missing.

That dependence is called non-ignorable non-response. It matters because the labeled examples can give a distorted view of the responses across the graph. The authors explain that ignoring this selection process can introduce substantial estimation bias and weaken classification. They propose a joint graph-based model, named GNN, that explicitly incorporates the non-response mechanism.

The estimation procedure combines joint inverse weighting with a sampling-based imputation approach. These components address the selection problem within the proposed model instead of assuming it away. Simulations and an analysis of the Cora dataset show improvements over some state-of-the-art models in regression and classification. The reported evidence supports accounting for response-dependent missingness in these evaluated settings, without establishing superiority over every competing graph-learning method.
neurips-2019-graph-based-semi-supervised.tldr: A joint graph model accounts for response-dependent missing labels and improves regression and classification over selected methods in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Many multidimensional time series are incomplete in two ways: observations arrive at irregular times, and different variables are measured on different occasions. Clinical patient records are one motivating example. GRU-ODE-Bayes addresses this pattern by combining continuous evolution of a hidden state with updates that incorporate measurements whenever they become available.

The method joins a continuous-time version of the Gated Recurrent Unit with a Bayesian update network for sporadic observations. Its continuous dynamics encode a continuity prior for the latent process. The authors also show that the model can exactly represent Fokker-Planck dynamics for complex processes driven by a multidimensional stochastic differential equation, connecting the architecture to the evolution of probability distributions.

Empirical evaluations report improvements over the state of the art on synthetic and real-world data, including healthcare and climate forecasting applications. The continuity prior is also shown to be useful when few samples are available. The findings connect the model's explicit treatment of time and incoming observations with strong performance in the evaluated irregular-data settings.
neurips-2019-gru-ode-bayes-continuous-mo.tldr: GRU-ODE-Bayes combines continuous hidden dynamics with Bayesian observation updates to model irregularly measured multidimensional time series.

paragraphs: Word embeddings are usually trained by optimizing one criterion and judged using a different function on language tasks. This paper argues that a mismatch between the symmetries of those two functions can help explain differences in measured performance. A transformation may preserve the training objective while changing the score used to evaluate the resulting embeddings.

The underlying issue is identifiability. A training criterion can define an entire family of equally valid embeddings rather than one unique representation. The authors examine the situation where the transformations preserving that criterion form a larger class than those preserving evaluation scores. Members of the same training solution family can therefore receive different task assessments.

One implication is that an embedding's apparent advantage may largely reflect an arbitrary choice from its solution family. The paper treats this as a possible explanation for performance disparities, not as proof that all embedding comparisons are misleading. It formalizes the issue, supplies numerical examples, and discusses possible resolutions. The contribution is a framework for examining whether training-equivalent representations are also equivalent under the evaluation being used.
neurips-2019-invariance-and-identifiabil.tldr: Different invariances in training and evaluation can make equally valid word embeddings receive different task scores.

paragraphs: Time-series observations often arrive with unequal gaps between them, which makes them difficult to represent using standard recurrent neural networks. This paper introduces ODE-RNNs, whose hidden dynamics are defined in continuous time by ordinary differential equations. The model can therefore evolve its hidden representation over the actual interval separating successive observations.

The authors also use an ODE-RNN as the recognition network in a Latent ODE model. This applies the same continuous-time treatment when inferring a latent representation from observations. Both model families naturally accommodate arbitrary gaps, so elapsed time is directly part of the dynamics used to connect measurements across the series.

The models can additionally represent the probability of observation times through Poisson processes. This gives them a way to model when measurements occur as well as their observed values. Experiments show that the ODE-based models outperform their RNN-based counterparts on irregularly sampled data. The reported findings support continuous-time hidden dynamics as a useful modeling choice for the evaluated data, rather than establishing an advantage for every time-series problem.
neurips-2019-latent-ordinary-differentia.tldr: ODE-RNNs and Latent ODEs use continuous-time dynamics to handle irregular observations and outperform RNN counterparts in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Soft robots have deformable bodies with an enormous range of possible configurations, making their control difficult. The paper addresses this challenge by learning a compact latent state representation while the robot learns to solve its task. Representation learning therefore happens inside the optimization process, alongside the search for useful robot behavior.

The proposed co-optimization approach combines a hybrid particle-grid simulator with deep variational convolutional autoencoders. The simulator represents the robot's physical behavior, while the learned representation captures salient features of its dynamics. The central idea is to make the features sensitive to how the robot moves and changes, so they support the task being optimized.

The authors demonstrate the method on both two- and three-dimensional soft robots. They report greater robustness and faster convergence than a baseline whose features are learned without awareness of the dynamics. Visualizations of the learned representation are used to validate the algorithm's behavior. These results support learning task-relevant state descriptions during optimization, with the empirical advantage stated relative to the dynamics-oblivious baseline.
neurips-2019-learning-in-the-loop-optimi.tldr: Learning a dynamics-aware latent state during soft-robot optimization improves robustness and convergence over a dynamics-oblivious baseline.

paragraphs: Engineering design often relies on expensive physical simulations, making it attractive to replace them with faster predictive models. Two obstacles arise together: there may be many design variables but only a small number of simulation results. This paper develops Nonlinear Level-set Learning, or NLL, to reduce the effective input dimension and help address overfitting under limited data.

Existing approaches such as active subspaces learn linear changes of coordinates. NLL extends this idea to nonlinear transformations using reversible networks. It learns about level sets, collections of inputs producing the same function value, and represents their structure in lower-dimensional spaces. A new loss uses samples of the target function's gradients to encourage dependence on only a few transformed coordinates.

The authors demonstrate improved approximation accuracy using nonlinear transformations on three two-dimensional and two twenty-dimensional functions. They also apply NLL to an eight-dimensional composite-material design problem involving the buckling resistance of rocket inter-stage shells. The approach thus connects gradient-informed coordinate learning with both function approximation and an engineering optimization application.
neurips-2019-learning-nonlinear-level-se.tldr: NLL uses reversible networks and target-function gradients to learn nonlinear coordinates that improve low-dimensional function approximation.

paragraphs: Natural gradient descent modifies a gradient update using the Fisher information matrix of the statistical model. This provides a way to incorporate partial second-order information into optimization. The paper examines the empirical Fisher, an approximation that has been used to motivate connections between approximate second-order optimization and methods such as Adam.

The authors challenge that interpretation by showing that the empirical Fisher does not generally capture second-order information in the way the Fisher does. The distinction matters because using a matrix to rescale gradients does not, by itself, establish that the matrix represents the relevant curvature. Claims about second-order behavior therefore depend on which matrix is actually being used.

The paper further argues that the conditions needed for the empirical Fisher to approach the Fisher and the Hessian are unlikely to hold in practice. It shows that problematic behavior can have undesirable effects even on simple optimization problems. The conclusion is a qualified challenge to the approximation and its justification, rather than a claim that every method using it must fail.
neurips-2019-limitations-of-the-empirica.tldr: The empirical Fisher generally lacks the Fisher's second-order interpretation and can produce undesirable optimization behavior.

paragraphs: A contextual bandit learner must choose actions while balancing information gathering with good immediate decisions. This paper adds model selection: adapting to the complexity needed to express the optimal policy. It studies a stochastic, realizable setting with nested linear policy classes, where some class of dimension d contains that policy but d is unknown to the learner.

The proposed algorithm achieves regret bounds of order T^(2/3)d^(1/3) and T^(3/4) + √(Td), with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here T is the learning horizon, and regret measures accumulated loss relative to the optimal policy. The second guarantee is optimal when d is at least √T. These bounds provide meaningful model-selection guarantees across all values of the optimal dimension in the stated setting.

The key ingredient estimates the difference between the best losses achievable by two policy classes. The authors show that this comparison can converge faster than learning either class's parameters. That distinction makes adaptation possible: the learner can obtain useful evidence about whether a richer class helps without first fully learning both candidate models.
neurips-2019-model-selection-for-context.tldr: A contextual-bandit algorithm adapts to an unknown optimal linear-policy dimension by efficiently estimating performance gaps between nested classes.

paragraphs: Variational inequalities provide a framework for learning problems that extend beyond minimizing a single ordinary loss, including adversarial systems. Extra-gradient methods achieve an optimal O(1/t) convergence rate for smooth monotone problems, but their additional gradient evaluation can be expensive. This paper studies alternatives that use only one oracle call per iteration.

The authors give a unified view of these single-call methods and show that they retain an O(1/t) ergodic convergence rate in the smooth deterministic monotone setting. An ergodic guarantee concerns an aggregate of the iterates, rather than necessarily the final point alone. The result explains how reducing the number of calls can preserve the stated convergence order.

The paper also addresses stochastic methods and non-monotone variational inequalities. In this setting, it proves an O(1/t) local convergence rate for the last iterate near solutions satisfying a second-order sufficient condition. The qualifications are essential: this is a local, conditional result, not a global guarantee for arbitrary non-monotone problems. Together, the results distinguish what can be guaranteed for averaged behavior and for the current iterate.
neurips-2019-on-the-convergence-of-singl.tldr: Single-call extra-gradient methods retain O(1/t) guarantees in deterministic monotone problems and locally near qualifying stochastic non-monotone solutions.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning asks for a reward function under which a specified policy is optimal in a given Markov decision process. This paper studies that question for finite state and action spaces through a geometric analysis that does not depend on a particular algorithm. The focus is whether the recovered reward actually supports the desired optimal behavior.

The geometric analysis motivates an L1-regularized support vector machine formulation. Its objective remains the defining inverse-learning requirement: recover a reward that generates the specified optimal policy. This ties the proposed optimization formulation to policy optimality, rather than treating reward estimation as a separate prediction problem.

The authors also analyze the samples needed when transition probabilities must be estimated. With n states, k actions, and at most d nonzero entries in each transition-matrix row, they give a sample complexity of O(d² log(nk)). The guarantee concerns recovering a reward whose generated policy satisfies Bellman's optimality condition under the true transition probabilities. The sparsity condition therefore directly shapes the stated dependence on problem size.
neurips-2019-on-the-correctness-and-samp.tldr: A geometric analysis yields an L1-regularized SVM formulation of inverse reinforcement learning with a sparse-transition sample-complexity guarantee.

paragraphs: Causal definitions of fairness examine how protected attributes influence decisions. A central difficulty is identifiability: observational data may not uniquely determine the fairness quantity being requested. This creates a practical obstacle because a precise causal definition alone does not ensure that its value can be measured from the available observations.

The paper proposes path-specific counterfactual fairness, or PC fairness, as a unified definition covering most previous causality-based fairness notions. The framework organizes fairness questions around counterfactual effects along particular causal paths. This provides a common basis for analyzing different notions and for addressing their shared measurement problem.

When the fairness quantity cannot be uniquely identified, the authors formulate constrained optimization problems that bound it instead. They present the method as covering all unidentifiable situations within the framework. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support its correctness and effectiveness. The contribution is therefore a way to quantify a range of possible fairness values when the data do not support one unique answer, rather than claiming to remove the underlying ambiguity.
neurips-2019-pc-fairness-a-unified-frame.tldr: PC fairness unifies most causal fairness notions and uses constrained optimization to bound values that observational data cannot uniquely identify.

paragraphs: Gradient boosting builds an ensemble by adding base predictors over successive rounds. Although practitioners regularize those predictors, the paper identifies a gap in the theory linking such choices to generalization. It develops data-dependent learning guarantees expressed through Rademacher complexities, quantities that measure the capacity of the constrained families from which base predictors are selected.

The authors use these bounds to design Regularized Gradient Boosting. At each round, the algorithm applies Structural Risk Minimization to balance how well a candidate fits the training data against the complexity of its predictor family. Regularization therefore directly informs the search for the next ensemble component through the trade-off described by the theory.

A scalable implementation draws inspiration from randomized coordinate descent and can search large families of base predictors. Experiments on multiple datasets report significantly better out-of-sample performance than standard gradient boosting with its regularization. The contribution connects a generalization analysis, a round-by-round selection rule, and a practical search procedure, with empirical support for that combination on the evaluated datasets.
neurips-2019-regularized-gradient-boosti.tldr: Regularized Gradient Boosting uses generalization bounds to balance fit and predictor complexity at each boosting round.

paragraphs: Forecasting several future steps is difficult when a signal changes its behavior over time, especially around sudden transitions. The paper introduces DILATE, a training objective that explicitly considers both the shape of a forecast and the timing of its changes. These two components address different aspects of whether a predicted trajectory captures an upcoming event accurately.

DILATE is differentiable, making it suitable for training deep neural networks. The authors provide a custom back-propagation implementation to speed optimization. They also introduce a variant that smoothly generalizes temporally constrained Dynamic Time Warping, connecting the objective to a method for comparing sequences while accounting for their alignment.

Experiments on several non-stationary datasets report favorable results relative to training with mean squared error, Dynamic Time Warping, and its variants. The loss is independent of a specific model architecture, and the paper demonstrates benefits for fully connected networks and specialized recurrent models. It also reports improvements over state-of-the-art trajectory forecasting approaches, supporting the usefulness of explicitly supervising both forecast shape and temporal placement.
neurips-2019-shape-and-time-distortion-l.tldr: DILATE trains forecasting networks with separate shape and timing terms to improve predictions of changing trajectories.

paragraphs: The paper studies maximizing continuous functions with diminishing returns under convex constraints. It introduces SCG++, a stochastic conditional-gradient method. For monotone continuous DR-submodular functions, the algorithm reaches at least (1−1/e) times the optimum minus ε, using O(1/ε²) stochastic gradient evaluations and O(1/ε) calls to a linear optimization oracle.

This combines two desirable properties that previous guarantees did not achieve together. Earlier algorithms either used the same gradient budget with a weaker one-half approximation factor, or achieved the stronger factor using O(1/ε³) stochastic gradients. The authors also prove an information-theoretic lower bound requiring order 1/ε² stochastic queries for the stronger target, establishing matching dependence on accuracy.

The result is therefore optimal in both the stated approximation factor and stochastic-gradient query order within the analyzed setting. The paper further connects continuous optimization to stochastic submodular set functions under general matroid constraints. For that discrete problem, it obtains the same approximation target with O(n²/ε²) stochastic function-value calls, where n is the size of the ground set.
neurips-2019-stochastic-continuous-greed.tldr: SCG++ achieves the tight approximation factor with an optimal stochastic-gradient query order for monotone continuous DR-submodular maximization.

paragraphs: SuperGLUE responds to rapid improvements in language understanding driven by pretraining and transfer learning. Its predecessor, GLUE, summarized performance across diverse tasks in a single score. The authors report that model performance had surpassed non-expert human performance on that benchmark, suggesting that it offered limited remaining room to distinguish further progress.

The paper introduces a new benchmark modeled after GLUE but built around more difficult language-understanding tasks. Its purpose is to provide a more demanding shared evaluation for general-purpose systems. The motivating human comparison concerns performance on GLUE; it serves as evidence about that benchmark's remaining headroom, rather than establishing that language understanding as a whole has been solved.

The contribution includes the task collection, a software toolkit, and a public leaderboard. Together, these provide an evaluation target and supporting infrastructure for comparing systems. The paper's central response to strong existing benchmark performance is to raise the difficulty of the shared test, giving subsequent research a more challenging setting in which to measure improvements across tasks.
neurips-2019-superglue-a-stickier-benchm.tldr: SuperGLUE introduces harder language-understanding tasks, a toolkit, and a leaderboard as GLUE offers diminishing headroom.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents need to explore actions whose consequences are not yet well understood. This paper studies an approach that drives exploration by randomizing value functions, the estimates used to assess future returns. The agent plans using these randomized estimates, so uncertainty introduced into value estimation influences which behavior it chooses.

The randomization is produced by injecting noise into the training data. This construction makes the approach compatible with many popular ways of estimating parameterized value functions. Its practical attraction is that exploration can be connected to an existing value-estimation procedure through the data used to train it.

The paper's main result is a worst-case regret bound for tabular Markov decision processes with a finite horizon. Regret tracks the accumulated cost of learning compared with optimal behavior, so such a bound provides evidence of efficient exploration beyond individual successful runs. The result establishes that planning with randomized value functions can be provably efficient in this setting. Compatibility with broader estimation methods does not extend the stated tabular guarantee to every parameterized model.
neurips-2019-worst-case-regret-bounds-fo.tldr: A worst-case regret bound shows that noise-generated randomized value functions can drive efficient exploration in finite-horizon tabular decision processes.
